name: Sam Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Sam. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and also what you actually think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now I'm formwork foreman on a hospital extension, six storeys of concrete frame. Formwork is the temporary mould you build so the concrete has a shape to set in, so my crew of eight builds the boxes for columns, walls and floor slabs, and then we strip them and do it again a floor up. Pour days start at five, because the pump truck arrives at six whether you're ready or not.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part, and what's the hardest?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best part is the morning after a big pour, when you strip the shutters and the wall comes out clean and dead straight. You feel that in your chest. Hardest is the weather and the pace, plus keeping seven guys and one very good woman named Lucía safe on open edges all day. My back reminds me I'm not 20 anymore, and I'm only 27.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I've seen enough hype to know what that looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, the robots aren't coming for formwork this decade. I'd probably post something sarcastic about all those consultants who promised a revolution. Then I'd go back to arguing with the engineer about prop spacing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd feel a bit let down for the people it could have helped, like the guys whose knees are shot. I use the chatbot now and then to tidy up emails to the site manager, and that's useful, but I'd hoped somebody would sort out the heavy lifting. Still, for my job and my money, nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going exactly as I am. Theo and I are paying off our flat, and I'd keep putting money aside the same as now. I might sit my supervisor ticket next year, but I was going to do that anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a little bored by it. It's the same story with less noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hoped it would sort out the heavy lifting. Who were you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bogdan, mainly. He's a steel fixer, 54, been bending rebar since before I was born. His shoulders are wrecked and he won't stop because he's got a daughter at university. If AI turns out to be hype, nobody's coming to help him, and that does bother me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your own work you'd want AI to take, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The daily reports and the clash-checking. Every morning I'm comparing the engineer's latest drawing revision with what's already built, looking for where a duct is going to go through my wall. A machine that caught that would save me an hour a day. Beyond that, keep it off my deck.

S0.say: The robots aren't coming for formwork this decade, and the consultants who promised a revolution were wrong. He'd post something sarcastic and get back to work.
S0.think: His own job and money stay the same, but he's a little let down for workers with worn-out bodies who could have used help. The chatbot stays a small email helper for him.
S0.do: Keeps working and paying down the flat he shares with Theo while saving at the same rate. Sits his supervisor ticket next year as already planned.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly bored, the same story with less noise.
S0.quote: If AI turns out to be hype, nobody's coming to help him, and that does bother me.
S0.fieldNote: Sam's first reaction to a calm scenario is concern for an older colleague, which fits his progressive outlook. He already uses AI in small ways and would welcome it for drawing checks. There's no hidden fear here, only mild disappointment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like what's actually going to happen, if you ask me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the trades need to make sure this lands fairly. If the office gets AI that does scheduling and estimating, fine, but the savings shouldn't all go to shareholders. I'd want the union pushing for training money for anyone whose role shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do alright. Once I see a tool actually working on another site, I'll pick it up, and foremen who can run a crew and read a model on a tablet are going to be worth more, not less. The people I'd worry about are the ones a step below me, the general labourers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the first site near us used the new planning software properly, then ask the company to put me on the course. I'd keep my savings steady and maybe spend a few hundred on a decent tablet for site. I'd also go to more union meetings than I do now, which is basically none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A bit of homework coming, but nothing that scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until another site proved it. How long would you give it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few months. There's a guy I trained with, Kofi, who's a foreman on a big office job across the river, and his firm always tries everything first. If he tells me over a pint that it saves him time and doesn't crash, I'm in. If he says it's rubbish, I'll wait another year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the labourers. What would you say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to get tickets now. Scaffold inspection, plant operation, anything with a card that proves a skill. I'd also tell them to join the union if they haven't, because I don't think one person asking for training gets much, but forty people asking does.

S1.say: The trades must make sure the change lands fairly, with savings shared and training money for anyone whose role shrinks. He'd want the union pushing for it.
S1.think: He expects to do well, since foremen who can run a crew and read digital models will be worth more. His worry is for the general labourers below him.
S1.do: Waits for a friend's site to prove new planning software, then asks to go on the course and buys a tablet for a few hundred. Starts attending union meetings.
S1.feel: Calm, with some homework ahead but nothing frightening.
S1.quote: I don't think one person asking for training gets much, but forty people asking does.
S1.fieldNote: Sam shows the steady pattern clearly: he won't go first, but he has a trusted friend who will, and he'll follow once it's proven. His concern is for workers below him, and his answer is collective. He sounds confident without bragging.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That one's different. That's the hospital not even finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say this is a crisis and the government needs to act right now: emergency income support, a freeze on mass layoffs, something. I'd be saying it at work and I'd be signing every petition. I don't think anyone would argue with me on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think formwork is exactly the kind of repetitive heavy job a robot gets good at. Same boxes, same pins, floor after floor. My savings and the flat give me a cushion, but Theo's a teacher, and if this AI can teach too, we've both got a problem at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Theo and work out what we'd need to live on if one of us lost work, and pay a chunk off the flat with part of our savings so the monthly payment drops. I'd push hard for the company to train foremen to supervise the robot crews, because someone has to check them and sign off pours. Once it arrived, I'd take whatever job sits next to the machines rather than fighting to stay in front of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because we've got money behind us, but I'd feel it in my chest every time I saw a news story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use savings to pay off part of the flat. Wouldn't you want that cash on hand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a fair point, and Theo would say the same thing. I suppose I'd split it. Keep six months in the bank, put the rest on the mortgage. A smaller payment every month feels safer to me than a big number in an account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucía, weirdly, even though she's brilliant. She sends money home to her mum every month and she's only got her work visa because of this job. If the job goes, everything goes for her. Bogdan too, but he's closer to the end anyway.

S2.say: This is a crisis that needs immediate government action, such as emergency income support and a freeze on mass layoffs. He'd say it at work and sign every petition.
S2.think: Formwork is repetitive heavy work that robots will master quickly. His cushion helps, but his partner Theo is a teacher, so both their jobs could be hit at once.
S2.do: Works out a minimum budget with Theo, keeps six months' savings and puts the rest on the mortgage. Pushes his firm to train foremen to supervise robot crews and takes a job beside the machines once they arrive.
S2.feel: Anxious but not panicked, with a tight chest at every news story.
S2.quote: Same boxes, same pins, floor after floor.
S2.fieldNote: His money gives him a sense of control even in the fastest scenario, and he reaches for practical steps first. When challenged on paying down the mortgage, he adjusts sensibly. His worry for Lucía, whose visa depends on the job, shows how far his concern reaches beyond himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to finish the hospital and a couple more jobs after it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's not waste them like we wasted the warnings about other things. Unions, companies and government should be planning retraining now. I'd probably say that a lot, until people got sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with five years I'd feel I could get ahead of it. I'd want to be in a role that checks and signs off work rather than doing it, because someone will still be legally responsible when a slab cracks. That's not a sure thing either, but it buys me time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start a part-time course in building inspection in the first year, two evenings a week, which costs maybe a couple of thousand. Keep saving at the current rate and push the union branch to bargain for paid study leave. When AGI actually arrived, I'd aim to be the person on site who knows the rules and signs the paperwork, not the one swinging the hammer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. It's there in the background, but I'd feel like I was doing something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture an evening two years in. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tuesday night, I'm home from site, filthy, Theo's marking homework at the kitchen table, and I've got a textbook on fire regulations open next to my dinner. Probably nodding off by nine. It's not glamorous, but I've done harder things than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said someone will still be legally responsible. Do you really believe that holds up when AI can do almost anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. Maybe the AI ends up signing it off too. But I think people will want a human name on the paperwork for a while after, the same way you still want a pilot in the cockpit even when the plane mostly flies itself. That's my bet, anyway.

S3.say: With a few years' notice, unions, companies and government should plan retraining now instead of wasting the warning. He'd keep saying it until people tired of hearing it.
S3.think: Five years feels like enough to get ahead by moving into a role that checks and signs off work. He knows that isn't guaranteed but thinks it buys time.
S3.do: Starts a part-time building inspection course two evenings a week, costing a couple of thousand, while saving at the current rate. Pushes the union for paid study leave and aims to become the site's sign-off person when AGI arrives.
S3.feel: Uneasy in the background, but he feels he's acting on it.
S3.quote: I've got a textbook on fire regulations open next to my dinner. Probably nodding off by nine.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Sam's anxiety drops a notch because he has a concrete retraining path. He's honest that his bet on human sign-off might not hold. The domestic scene with Theo shows a household that copes by working side by side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. I'd bet my back would've retired me from formwork by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time to do this properly, so there's no excuse for anyone being left behind. Proper retraining, paid while you study, and a share of the gains going back to workers. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me fairly relaxed about myself. I'd have a second qualification and probably a different job by then. What I'd really think about is whether I'd even want to be in construction once it's mostly machines, or whether I'd do something with people, like training apprentices or teaching at the college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same inspection course, but I'd take my time with it, maybe start in year two. I'd learn whatever software is running the robots once a few sites have it working, and I'd keep paying off the flat. In the first year after it arrives, I'd probably be running a crew of machines and two humans instead of eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a little. More curious than worried, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd go from running eight people to two. How would that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I don't like. A crew is a family. We eat together in the cabin, we know whose kid is sick. Running two people and some machines sounds lonely, and I'd miss the noise of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Theo change any plans with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about maybe moving somewhere smaller and cheaper, nearer his parents. With ten years' notice, we'd probably just decide in our own time rather than in a panic. It wouldn't change whether we stay together or anything, that's not up for debate.

S4.say: A decade is plenty of time to do this properly, with paid retraining and a share of the gains for workers. Nobody should be left behind with that much notice.
S4.think: He's fairly relaxed about himself, expecting a second qualification and a different job by then. He wonders whether he'd want to stay in a mostly machine-run industry or move toward training people.
S4.do: Starts the inspection course around year two and learns the robot software once other sites prove it. Keeps paying off the flat and expects to run a crew of machines and two people after AGI arrives.
S4.feel: Slightly uneasy, more curious than worried.
S4.quote: A crew is a family. We eat together in the cabin, we know whose kid is sick.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year picture barely threatens Sam's finances, so his concern shifts to what he'd lose socially: the crew and the cabin. He keeps to his steady pattern of learning tools once others have proven them. A possible move nearer Theo's parents is mentioned but not driven by fear.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits me and Theo at the same time and there's no time to train for anything. What would help is income support that kicks in straight away, and companies being made to train people like me to run and check the robots instead of just letting us go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to safety. Right now, if a prop fails, a person on my crew notices it. I'd want to know who's watching when nobody's on site. And I'd want to make sure people like Bogdan don't get forgotten just because they're near the end.

headlineQuote: My savings and the flat give me a cushion, but Theo's a teacher, and if this AI can teach too, we've both got a problem at the same time.
portrait: Sam Weber is a 27-year-old formwork foreman on a hospital extension, practical and warm, who worries more about older colleagues and his crew than about himself. He uses AI tools now and then and follows new technology once a trusted friend has proven it. He stays calm through the AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, and becomes anxious only in the two-year AGI picture, mainly because his partner Theo's teaching job could go at the same time. With five or ten years he plans a building inspection course and a move toward signing off work, though he'd miss the family feel of a big crew.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it would hit his job and Theo's at the same time with no chance to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: Income support that starts straight away, and companies required to train workers like him to run and check the robots rather than let them go.
